headline: High-risk data exfiltration and compliance mismatch: RD-Agent’s broad egress can leak PDF inputs while pdf.js provides no containment.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: pdf.js ingests PDF files and can run browsers, while RD-Agent also runs browsers and processes research artifacts. A malicious PDF could carry instruction-like content that RD-Agent later treats as input if outputs are bridged manually or via shared files. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven.
conditions: IF pdf.js output is copied into RD-Agent prompts or files
IF a shared workspace or clipboard bridges PDF-derived text into RD-Agent
mitigations: Keep pdf.js and RD-Agent in separate workspaces
Disable copy-paste of extracted PDF text into agent prompts
Review PDF-derived text before passing it onward
Use a manual approval step before RD-Agent consumes any pdf.js output

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js handles PDF documents locally, but RD-Agent has broad network egress and sends data to external APIs by default. If PDF contents from pdf.js are forwarded into RD-Agent, sensitive document text can leave the local environment. The pair therefore creates a realistic exfiltration path with irreversible disclosure risk.
conditions: IF PDF contents from pdf.js are passed into RD-Agent
IF RD-Agent uses its configured API backends on those contents
mitigations: Do not route sensitive PDFs into RD-Agent
Run RD-Agent with network egress blocked for sensitive jobs
Redact PDFs before any handoff
Use separate credentials and workspaces
requires-engineering: add egress allowlisting and content classification gates

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and both can run browsers, so concurrent access to shared files or browser state could conflict if orchestrated together. pdf.js writes only PDF files, while RD-Agent writes logs and uses external APIs; overlapping mutable state is not documented, but uncertainty about shared workspace handling warrants a medium rating.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory
IF browser profiles or temp files are shared between them
mitigations: Use distinct directories for each agent
Separate browser profiles and temp paths
Serialize access to any shared artifacts
Avoid concurrent writes to the same log or output tree

D_cascading_error.rationale: RD-Agent can consume research inputs and act through API-backed workflows, while pdf.js produces document content that may be treated as authoritative text. If pdf.js output is fed into RD-Agent without verification, errors or malformed extraction can cascade into downstream actions. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF pdf.js extracted text is used as RD-Agent input
IF RD-Agent acts on that text without a verification step
mitigations: Insert a human verification step before handoff
Require source-document citations for extracted claims
Compare extracted text against the original PDF
Limit RD-Agent to read-only analysis for pdf-derived inputs

E_compliance.rationale: pdf.js is a local document processor, but RD-Agent requests multiple external API keys and broad egress, so regulated PDF content can cross into third-party services. Because pdf.js touches PDF documents and RD-Agent handles financial reports, logs, and research data, the pair can create a compliance breach if sensitive or residency-bound documents are processed through RD-Agent.
conditions: IF PDFs contain regulated data such as financial or personal information
IF RD-Agent forwards that content to external APIs
mitigations: Exclude regulated PDFs from RD-Agent workflows
Use a local-only model for sensitive documents
Add a data-classification gate before handoff
Document retention and residency rules for both tools
requires-engineering: enforce policy-based routing by data class
